title: What NOT to do during a cut
summary: Explains what a cut is and warns against cutting too fast, using his own crash cut from 240 to 210 lbs as a cautionary tale. Argues naturals should be patient, avoid 'lean goggles', and aim to enjoy their body year-round by recomping rather than cycling between big bulks and crash cuts.

claims.claim: He has mostly perma-bulked his whole lifting career and only had a few stints of cutting.
A cut is reducing calories to lose body mass; for a natural that mass is fat, water and muscle, and the goal is to lose as much fat and as little muscle as possible.
You don't deliberately cut water unless prepping for a show, but since fat holds water you will lose some water as you lose fat.
A proper cut makes you more defined and dry; pumped and shirtless you won't look smaller even after losing 10-20 lbs, because fat hid muscle definition.
Fatty big arms that are cut down are objectively smaller on the tape measure but won't look smaller to the untrained eye.
The thing to avoid in a cut is the body cannibalising muscle; for naturals that's not hard to avoid as long as they are patient.
Two- or three-month cuts are too fast in his opinion, unless it's a mini-cut or you are only losing a few pounds.
Trying to lose a pound a week is too fast, just like trying to gain a pound a week is too fast; both ignore what the body can realistically do in a short time.
He bulked to 240 lbs, got scared when he realised he was fat, and crash-cut 30 lbs to 210 in about five months, losing fat and water but also muscle.
The fast cut was mentally awful because he lost a lot of strength; strength loss isn't proof of muscle loss, but serious lifters find the two hard to separate in their minds.
Bulking to 240 lbs was a mistake in the first place.
If you messed up and got fat, accept the punishment: you will be fat for a long time because you should cut down very slowly.
If your body image is hurting your mental health you can do a 'suicide cut', but know it is not optimal and is dangerous for your health.
After the traumatic cut to 210 he recomped, did a mini-bulk to 225, then decided to be smarter and has been recomping for a year and a half, now around 215 lbs.
Don't rush your weight loss, just as you shouldn't rush weight gain; even show-preppers should have planned better rather than rushing.
Beware 'lean goggles' on a cut, the mirror image of size goggles on a bulk: you see abs and lost love handles but not the size you're losing everywhere else.
A smart cut should not leave you looking shrunken, depleted and flat.
Everything worth having and admiring takes time; crash dieting produces a disappointing physique.
Without discipline you get stuck in an endless cycle of bulking too high and cutting too low, never enjoying your body.

For him being a natural bodybuilder means enjoying his body all year: not hiding fat in winter nor feeling small in clothes in summer; staying lean while slowly losing fat and adding muscle is the best natural approach.
